video_title: The Battle of the Bridges - The Crimean Bridge & Russia's Strike Campaign
gist: Perun analyses the November 2026 'Battle of the Bridges': Ukraine's multi-wave saturation strike (hundreds of drones, Dutch mini cruise missiles, Neptunes and FPV-guided Flamingo missiles over a mesh network) that collapsed the Kerch Strait road span, versus Russia's Iskander-led strikes on Dnipro bridges in Kyiv. He argues the value of bridge strikes hinges on munition opportunity costs and redundancy, and that Ukraine's strike capacity (with plans to triple deep strike in 2027) is scaling fast while the war looks set to run into 2027.

insights.claim: Russia's frontline gains have slowed to very limited or even net-negative while claimed Russian personnel losses keep spiking, yet Moscow is still pressing maximalist demands (rest of the Donbas fortress belt, NATO rollbacks), creating a major disconnect between demands and military leverage.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: A wide negotiation gap implies no near-term ceasefire; price continued war risk premia in defence, energy and Black Sea-linked assets.
insights.quote: it still seems likely that Russia is pushing fairly maximalist war goals without maximalist frontline results to back them

insights.claim: Russia reportedly rejected a Turkish-floated Black Sea agreement that would have let grain, fertilizer and energy exports on civilian vessels reach world markets, signalling Moscow judges the economic pain on Ukraine worth its own costs.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Black Sea shipping de-risking for grain/fertilizer/energy exports is not imminent; keep risk premia in freight and ag-commodity supply assumptions.

insights.claim: With demands unsoftened, both sides seek leverage via the front line and via long-range strike campaigns that apply military, economic, social and humanitarian pressure; November 2026 has been exceptionally intense on the strike side.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Expect sustained high munition consumption and infrastructure damage through winter, supporting demand for drones, missiles and air defence.

insights.claim: Perun expects the war to continue through the 2026 heating season and into 2027 given the gap at the negotiating table, with winter typically being the peak of the long-range strike 'pain' campaign while ground offensives slow due to lost foliage concealment.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Position for a 2027 war scenario: continued Ukrainian grid damage, Russian refinery hits and elevated defence procurement.
insights.quote: I think it's fair to assume the war is going to continue through the heating season of 2026 and into 2027

insights.claim: Putin said after the Crimean Bridge strike that Russia 'will not negotiate, we will respond', but Perun argues such statements are likely an excuse to refuse terms Russia already rejected rather than a real shift.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Discount escalation rhetoric as a driver of negotiation outcomes; underlying positions are what matter for peace-deal timing bets.

insights.claim: Ideal strike targets are valuable, easy to destroy and hard to regenerate (ammo dumps, large e-commerce warehouses like Wildberries-style, data centers, refineries/oil storage); reinforced concrete bridges tick only the 'valuable' box.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Useful lens for judging which infrastructure (energy, logistics, data centers) is most exposed to drone/missile campaigns.

insights.claim: Russia's October 3-4 jet-drone strikes on a Kyiv bridge were repaired with the bridge back in operation by October 6, i.e. two waves of expensive munitions bought roughly two days of disruption.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Strikes on redundant concrete infrastructure have poor cost-effectiveness; repair capacity, not just air defence, is a key resilience variable.
insights.quote: Two waves of attacks to roughly take a bridge out of action for 2 days.

insights.claim: On the bridge linking Odesa region directly to Romania (bypassing Moldova), most hits by drones, glide bombs and Onyx missiles caused only a couple of days of disruption; the longest outages came from the Kh-22's roughly one-ton warhead, and Ukrainian repair crews have grown faster since 2022.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Warhead size, not munition count, determines bridge outcomes; Ukraine's western logistics corridor to Romania is resilient.

insights.claim: In a war of resource shortages, using costly precision munitions to make temporary road-surface holes is a poor trade, which partly explains why both sides had previously held back on bridge campaigns rather than taboos alone.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Munition allocation is driven by cost-per-effect; expect shifts in target sets to track munition availability and warhead size.
insights.quote: In a war of resource shortages, excavating million-dollar potholes can be a significant investment

insights.claim: Escalation should be split into escalation of means and of target type; both Russia and Ukraine are close to conventionally maxed out, so political shocks can only bring forward or surge strikes short-term before supply constraints bind again.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Don't expect sustained step-changes in strike volume from political events; production capacity is the binding constraint to track.
insights.quote: both sides are pretty close to conventionally maxed out

insights.claim: Ukraine's many redundant Dnipro bridges may be acting as a 'munition sponge', absorbing scarce premium Russian munitions like enhanced Iskanders that could otherwise hit more painful targets, much as Russian bridges once absorbed Storm Shadow and SCALP missiles.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russia's bridge campaign may be lower-value than headlines imply; watch whether it diverts strikes from grid and industry.

insights.claim: Ukraine destroyed a full span of the Kerch Strait road bridge using hundreds of one-way attack drones, Dutch mini cruise missiles, Neptunes and at least three Flamingo cruise missiles in three waves: air-defence suppression, a radio-relay drone wave, then the heavy strike package.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Demonstrates Ukraine can now penetrate even the most heavily defended Russian assets, raising risk to other high-value Russian infrastructure.

insights.claim: The road and rail arches weigh roughly 5,000-6,000 tons each, and installing the rail arch in 2017 took specialised equipment and most of a month without drone attacks, so road bridge repair is a major engineering problem.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Expect a prolonged road-bridge outage, raising Crimea supply costs and shifting load to rail and the land corridor.
insights.quote: The road and rail arches reportedly weigh something like 5 to 6,000 tons each

insights.claim: The collapsed road span blocks the channel under the bridge, cutting Russia's ability to move ships between the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov until it is cleared.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Disrupts Azov-Black Sea shipping routes for Russian commercial and military vessels; watch for clearance timelines.

insights.claim: The strategically more important rail bridge survived with less damage; trains resumed under apparent speed/weight restrictions, then were suspended again after a smaller follow-up Neptune strike on the rail bridge.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: The rail bridge's fate is the key variable for Crimea supply, including fuel; further Ukrainian attempts are likely.

insights.claim: Russia can sustain Crimea without one of its three supply routes (sea, Kerch bridges, land corridor through occupied Kherson/Zaporizhzhia) but not without all three, so the strike's value depends on what happens to the rail bridge and the mid-strike fight on the land route.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Monitor rail-bridge status and land-corridor interdiction as leading indicators of Crimea fuel/goods shortages.
insights.quote: What they couldn't realistically manage is being without all three.

insights.claim: Russia has restricted fuel shipments over the Crimean Bridge to limit risk but has run fuel trains anyway when desperate (e.g., June 2024), so loss of rail capacity would directly hit Crimea fuel supply.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Crimea fuel availability is exposed to rail-bridge damage; watch for regional fuel shortages and price spikes.

insights.claim: The R280 highway, built by Russia during the war as a Crimean Bridge alternative, was designed before Ukrainian mid-range strike drones were a threat; more truck traffic there would force Russia to divert more air defence and Ukraine to divert more drones.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Expect intensified interdiction along the land bridge, raising Russian logistics costs and counter-drone demand.

insights.claim: Perun judges the Kerch strike 'probably' worth it versus the opportunity cost of hitting refineries, arguing many senior Russian decision-makers would trade a couple of burning refineries to undo it.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Signals Ukraine's target priorities can shift from energy to logistics nodes; refinery-strike rates may vary accordingly.

insights.claim: Pro-Russian commentators mocked the first wave's damage, but the shortage of visible surface-to-air missile fire against easily intercepted Flamingos suggests the early waves suppressed or exhausted Russian air defences around the bridge.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russian air-defence capacity in Crimea is degraded and stretched, increasing vulnerability of Crimean assets.

insights.claim: Ukraine no longer needs quiet stockpiling periods before big saturation raids: during the bridge operation it kept hitting refineries every couple of days and airfields, with Russia claiming 1,336 drones launched in the first wave, 600 toward Moscow.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russian energy assets face sustained, not episodic, strike pressure; refinery outages are likely to persist.
insights.quote: the Russians claimed the Ukrainians launched 1,336 drones, of which 600 went to Moscow

insights.claim: The recent rate of Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries is well up again, and October 2026 was a record month for Russian fuel imports.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russian refining disruption is tightening domestic fuel supply, relevant to product cracks and regional fuel trade flows.
insights.quote: October was notably a record month for Russian fuel imports

insights.claim: Because the air defence needed to guarantee any single target's safety scales with the opponent's launch capacity, Ukraine's growing volumes force Russia to thicken defences everywhere (Moscow rings, Putin's Valdai residence) at the expense of places like Crimea.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russian demand for air defence systems outstrips production; expect continued thin coverage of energy and logistics sites.

insights.claim: Ukraine's defence minister told the 37th Ukraine Defense Contact Group in Brussels that Ukraine plans to triple its deep strike capabilities in 2027 and expand joint weapon production with European nations.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Tailwind for European defence firms in joint production with Ukraine and for long-range drone/missile supply chains; Perun cautions targets may be partly empty.

insights.claim: Ukraine's one-way attack force is diversifying: cheap propeller drones for bulk, Ukrainian jet drones like Palonitsa, imported mini cruise missiles (Ruta/'routter' from the Netherlands, Rusty Dagger from the US), and possible future ballistic missiles like Nightfall or FP9.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Mini cruise missile and jet-drone makers are gaining a real market; watch Western suppliers of low-cost strike munitions.

insights.claim: A Dutch defence company openly publicised its mini cruise missile's use against the Kerch bridge, a stark shift from earlier years of NATO hesitancy over Taurus, ATACMS and Tomahawk.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Western political appetite for supplying and marketing strike weapons to Ukraine has grown; supports export sales for European missile makers.

insights.claim: Zelensky named 12 distinct systems involved in the bridge strike, and Ukraine is combining them (e.g., the light long-range drone used as an FPV carrier against SAMs and radars) to find the most economical ways to exhaust or evade air defences.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: System-of-systems integration, not single platforms, is the competitive edge; favours suppliers that interoperate within strike packages.

insights.claim: Fire Point's Flamingo is a ~6-ton, non-stealthy, often inaccurate ground-launched cruise missile with a ~1-ton warhead that is usually intercepted, making it a 'gambling mechanic' that occasionally lands very damaging hits.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Evaluate Ukrainian domestic missile makers on effective hit rate in combined packages, not standalone specs; Firepoint has a commercial incentive to oversell.
insights.quote: So basically for Ukraine, the missile has often been a gambling mechanic.

insights.claim: Ukraine appears to have flown Flamingo with manual, FPV-style man-in-the-loop guidance to solve its accuracy problem, effectively a six-ton FPV, scoring a clean hit that collapsed the road span.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Human-in-the-loop guidance upgrades cheap, inaccurate missiles into precision weapons, lowering the cost of precision strike.

insights.claim: Perun considers the communications link the most important revelation: Ukraine maintained a high-quality, low-latency link to weapons near the heavily jammed bridge without Starlink/Starshield (limited above ~161 km/h and reportedly jammed), likely via an airborne mesh network of relay drones.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Reduces Ukraine's dependence on SpaceX connectivity and blunts Russian EW; mesh-networking and resilient datalink tech is a key defence-tech growth area.

insights.claim: If mesh-networked strike comms can be refined and scaled, Russian reliance on existing EW such as Starlink jammers weakens, and weapons with significant weaknesses can overperform by flying lower under continuous operator control.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Watch for counter-EW and relay-drone adoption; Crimea and near-front Russian assets face rising risk.

insights.claim: Western restrictions such as limits on Star Shield over Russian territory show Russia's rhetorical red lines, though mostly hollow, have still succeeded in getting Western states to modulate support and pressure Ukraine on strike types.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Policy restrictions on tech providers remain a material constraint on Ukraine's strike effectiveness; watch policy shifts by US providers.

insights.claim: A recent large Russian attack reportedly included 84 cruise missiles, 400+ one-way attack drones and just under 30 ballistic missiles, hitting among other things three Kyiv bridges over the Dnipro.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Russia retains a volume advantage in long-range fire; Ukrainian infrastructure and economy remain under heavy pressure.
insights.quote: 84 cruise missiles, more than 400 oneway attack drones, and just under 30 reported ballistic missiles

insights.claim: Russia's Iskander ballistic missiles, possibly upgraded with terminal-phase target-recognition seekers, are doing much of the heavy lifting, and Ukraine's Patriot interceptor supply remains critical with no real alternatives yet.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Ballistic-missile-defence interceptors are the scarcest asset in Ukraine; supports demand for Patriot/PAC-3 and alternative ABM programs.
insights.quote: Patriot interceptor supplies remain critical and the alternatives just aren't really there yet.

insights.claim: Russian attacks have hit Ukraine's power grid and critical utilities repeatedly, and Zelensky reported Ukraine's biggest steel plant has been at least temporarily taken offline.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Ukrainian industrial output (steel) and power availability face winter disruption; relevant to steel trade and reconstruction demand.

insights.claim: Russia's Dnipro bridge campaign faces far greater redundancy than Ukraine's Kerch target: many bridges, heavy Kyiv air defences, and quick partial reopenings mean its strategic payoff is much less certain despite greater firepower.
insights.speaker: Perun (host)
insights.so_what: Don't over-read Kyiv bridge strikes as decisive for Ukrainian logistics; grid strikes are the bigger economic threat.
